This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 39-1014.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Entertainment and Recreation Workers, Except Gambling Services” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation, and the body text follows that official occupational scope). Even within on-site supervision, the differences are large: gyms and sports venues, water parks and swimming facilities, theme parks and amusement parks, camps and outdoor recreation, community and public cultural and sports venues, beauty and leisure service stores, and event and visitor experience services; a supervisor may lead only one shift or simultaneously manage several positions and venues. Before comparing positions or development paths, first check: the education and experience required for the role, whether specialty qualifications such as lifeguarding or equipment operation are required, on-site safety and first aid training requirements, working hours and scheduling arrangements (including weekends and holidays), and whether independent venue or store management responsibility is required.

Validate with one paper exercise: you are given a completely fictitious leisure venue operating assignment (venue type and floor area, opening hours and expected customer flow for the day, the number of employees on shift and their positions, the activities or classes to be organized, available equipment and supplies, a customer complaint or equipment safety hazard, and the records and reporting to be completed). You are asked to write out the shift schedule and position assignments, facility and equipment inspection key points, activity organization and safety reminders, the complaint handling and escalation path, and the records and reports to be used, and to mark which decisions must be made by the venue manager or personnel with specialty qualifications.

Signals worth considering more: willingness to deal with customers and employees over the long term, patience under customer flow peaks and complaint pressure, and willingness to manage scheduling and on-site order according to rules. Signals requiring caution: unwillingness to work weekends and holidays, difficulty handling customer conflicts or employee discipline problems, and imagining work in the leisure industry as playing all the time yourself.
This card is a career exploration reference and does not constitute hiring, ability scoring, safety, or compliance conclusions.

First judge whether you are willing to make on-site management of a leisure and service venue a long-term career: it requires working weekends and holidays, arranging shifts and positions according to institutional rules, organizing activities and handling customer complaints, and bearing supervisory responsibility for facility and equipment safety and employee service performance; validate with the paper exercise and seven-day task on this page.

The work of first-line supervisors of entertainment and recreation workers revolves around the cycle of “pre-open preparation—scheduling and division of labor—on-site patrol and activity organization—customer and employee issue handling—records and improvement”: before opening, check facility and equipment status, whether supplies and safety items are in place, and confirm the day's activity schedule; arrange shifts and position assignments according to customer flow and opening hours, and explain service standards and work processes to employees; during opening hours, patrol facilities and equipment, verify cleanliness and maintenance standards, and organize sports, aquatic, game, or performance activities with safety reminders; handle customer complaints and on-site employee issues, providing assistance or taking disciplinary action according to rules when necessary; requisition equipment and supplies, record personnel and operating data and write activity reports, and take part in training to keep up with industry changes. The emphasis differs greatly by direction: the fitness and sports venue direction stresses classes and equipment safety, the aquatic and amusement direction stresses lifeguarding and equipment inspection, the camp and outdoor direction stresses activity organization and outdoor safety, the community and public cultural and sports venue direction stresses public order and activity scheduling, and the leisure service store direction stresses service standards and employee performance management.

U.S. O*NET-SOC 39-1014.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Entertainment and Recreation Workers, Except Gambling Services”: directly supervise and coordinate the work of entertainment and recreation related service workers.

Main objects | Customers and members, staff on shift and temporary workers, facilities and equipment, gear and supplies, activity and class schedules, complaint and feedback records, and operating and personnel data.

Tools and materials | Scheduling and attendance software, inventory management software, office and spreadsheet software, facility and equipment inspection forms, safety and first aid supplies, activity and class schedules, and complaint and operating records.

Environment and pace | Opening hours and customer flow peaks determine work intensity, and weekends and holidays are usually the busiest; the site involves customer conflicts, equipment and aquatic activity risks, and long periods of standing and walking.

entries.answer: This page is written according to the U.S. O*NET-SOC 39-1014.00 “First-Line Supervisors of Entertainment and Recreation Workers, Except Gambling Services” (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese occupational name for this occupation): directly supervise and coordinate the work of entertainment and recreation related service workers. Specifically this includes: before opening, checking facility and equipment status, supplies and safety items, and confirming the day's activity schedule; arranging shifts and position assignments according to customer flow and opening hours and explaining service standards and work processes to employees; during opening hours, patrolling facilities and equipment, verifying cleanliness and maintenance standards, and organizing sports, aquatic, game, or performance activities with safety reminders; handling customer complaints and on-site employee issues and, when necessary, providing assistance or taking disciplinary action according to rules; requisitioning equipment and supplies; recording personnel and operating data and writing activity reports; and taking part in continuing education to keep up with industry changes.
entries.question: What do First-Line Supervisors of Entertainment and Recreation Workers, Except Gambling Services mainly do?

entries.answer: Primary tasks and management scope differ: this occupation's main output is shift and position management of service workers within a venue, activity organization, and on-site issue handling, and it is a first-line management position; entertainment and recreation attendants produce direct guidance, ticketing, and equipment service; entertainment and recreation managers focus on overall venue operation, budgets, and marketing with a larger management scope; fitness trainers and group fitness instructors produce class design and instruction; meeting, convention, and event planners focus on event plans and vendor coordination; food service managers focus on restaurant operation and compliance; lodging managers focus on accommodation operation and room management; and ushers focus on greeting and ticket checking.

entries.answer: The more accurate judgment is that steps such as scheduling and attendance statistics, inventory and supply requisitioning, activity registration and feedback aggregation, and report and training material drafting will be taken over by tools, and the occupation as a whole will mainly see augmentation. The ILO 2023 study shows that task exposure varies greatly across occupations, that the share of highly exposed tasks in managerial and professional occupations is relatively low, and that technical feasibility does not mean agencies have already adopted it; on-site safety judgment, employee management, and service responsibility must be borne by trained personnel with authority, so the conclusion is that the way of working will change, not that the occupation as a whole will be replaced.

subject.summary: Directly supervise and coordinate the work of entertainment and recreation service workers: includes arranging shifts and position assignments, training employees and explaining work processes according to company rules, patrolling facilities and equipment to verify cleanliness and maintenance standards, organizing sports, aquatic, game, and performance activities, handling customer complaints and improving service, requisitioning equipment and supplies, evaluating employee performance and taking disciplinary action, and recording personnel and operating data and writing activity reports.
